title: He had the looks.
paragraphs:
He had the looks.
The influence.
The moment.

Scripture says there was no flaw in his appearance from head to foot (2 Samuel 14:25).
Charisma radiated from him. Presence. Power. The kind that turns heads without trying.

Not with rebellion.
Not with war.

A justice delayed.
A father who didn’t act fast enough.
A heart that learned how to smile in public…
while bleeding in private.
So he stepped into the gate.

Not with violence—
but with strategy.

He listened.
He affirmed.
He sympathized.
“He stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” (2 Samuel 15:6)

Because some victories don’t come from truth—
but from manipulation dressed as compassion.
This is where it gets dangerous.

Fifty men ran before him.
Momentum built.
Influence expanded.

Turned into ambition.
Then ambition into rebellion.
Then rebellion into self-coronation.

No oil.
No prophet.
No God.

David fled Jerusalem barefoot, weeping (2 Samuel 15:30).
The palace shook.
The throne looked vulnerable.
Absalom was inches away from everything he ever wanted.
But here’s the truth we don’t like to hear:

If God didn’t give it—
you can’t keep it.
The battlefield shifted to the forest.

Not a palace.
Not a throne room.
Just like the consequences of unchecked ambition.

Riding fast.
Hair flowing.
Confidence high.

The very thing that made him admired…
became the thing that trapped him.

The man who stole hearts
lost his life.
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son…”
Because rebellion doesn’t just destroy the rebel—
It wounds everyone who loves them.
Because this story isn’t ancient history.

God gives vision.
God raises leaders.
God entrusts influence.
But when ambition is no longer submitted to God—

“I deserve this.”
“I can do it better.”
“They don’t see my worth.”
You stop asking what God wants…
And start chasing what you want.
That’s where Absalom fell—long before the tree.
Because this is where everything changes.

Where Absalom reached for a throne—
Jesus Christ walked toward a cross.

Where Absalom lifted himself in pride—
Jesus humbled Himself in obedience.
“He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.”
And here’s the scandal of grace:

Even if you’ve been building your own throne…
Even if your motives have been mixed…
Even if pride has been quietly ruling your decisions—
Because the cross doesn’t just forgive sin.

The same Jesus who obeyed perfectly
offers mercy completely.
Will you keep building something God never anointed?

Or will you lay it down
and let Him rebuild you?

Don’t wait until the fall
to recognize the root.

Don’t wait until the consequences
to confront the condition.

Not later.
Not when it’s convenient.

Lay down the image.
Lay down the control.
Lay down the silent pride.
Because Jesus doesn’t just rescue you from falling—

Before what you’re chasing
costs you more than you’re willing to lose.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
